:::

```{=html}
<div id="x03-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- x03-ideas:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>Decades, not years</dt><dd>On its <span class="lx-term" data-term="diffusion-curve">diffusion curve</span>, electric service went from 8% of U.S. homes in 1907 to over 90% between 1945 and 1950.</dd><dt>Not everywhere at once</dt><dd>Farms passed half about 25 years after town homes; wires had to reach them first.</dd><dt>A rise is also a fall</dt><dd>Utility gas replaced coal as the main home heating fuel between the 1950 and 1960 censuses.</dd><dt>What sped it</dt><dd>Networks built, public programmes and a cheaper or better service; a slow start in niche markets held new sources back.</dd><dt>Say what you measure</dt><dd>A device in homes, a fuel's share of a nation and a share of electricity move at different speeds.</dd></dl>
<!-- x03-ideas:end -->
</div>
</div>
<!-- x03-stop:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-card xs-stop" id="x03-stop"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Where we stop</p><h3>This side topic stops at reading the curves</h3><p class="xs-stop-lede">Adoption enters the course only as diffusion, a share over time; costs and forecasts stay out.</p><div class="xs-stop-cols"><div><h4 class="xs-h">This side topic covers</h4><ul><li>What share of homes, families or electricity each change reached, and when.</li><li>What sped some curves up and held others back, read from dated sources.</li><li>Why the answer to 'how fast' depends on what you measure.</li></ul></div><div><h4 class="xs-h">Left to specialists</h4><ul><li>How the cost of any technology changed over time.</li><li>Forecasts of how fast anything spreads next.</li><li>Economic history beyond these curves: prices, wages, trade.</li></ul></div></div><h4 class="xs-h">Read next, three rungs</h4><ol class="xs-ladder"><li><b>Start here.</b> Long-run charts of the world's energy sources, with how each series is built. <span class="xs-src"><a href="https://ourworldindata.org/energy">Our World in Data, Energy: Energy Sources and Transitions (Ritchie, Rosado and Roser)</a>, published 20 December 2023, read 7 November 2026</span></li><li><b>Go further.</b> How long national and global transitions took, country by country. <span class="xs-src">Vaclav Smil, Energy Transitions: Global and National Perspectives (Praeger), cited by name, second edition, 2017</span></li><li><b>Go deep.</b> Energy across human history, from muscle power to fossil fuels and electricity. <span class="xs-src">Vaclav Smil, Energy and Civilization: A History (MIT Press), cited by name, 2017</span></li></ol></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Reading a diffusion curve without fooling yourself</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Say the whole.** A share of homes, of families and of electricity are three different wholes; a curve means nothing until its denominator is named.
- **Published points only.** The page reports a year as "between 1945 and 1950" rather than drawing a smooth line through gaps.
- **Starts and ends.** The car survey began when most families already had a car; solar's curve stops at the latest year of data.
- **Services first.** Grubler (2012, abstract) points to energy end use and services, and to the lengthy process of transitions.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>

<li>Prices, wages and trade: the economic history behind each curve.</li>
<li>How the cost of any technology changed over time.</li>
<li>Any forecast of how fast a curve will move next.</li>
</ul>
```
